Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-30
Time: 15:30 UTC (approx)
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Martinez (Redwood AE), Ethan Cho (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (Crestline Lead ML Eng), Daniel Cho (Crestline Backend), Liam O'Neill (CTO)

---- Auto summary (auto notes) ----
Quick demo of Redwood hosted chat/text generation: streaming behavior, parameter tuning (temperature, max_tokens), retry/backoff strategies, idempotency, and console hints from Optimize. Security topics: SOC2, KMS, retention. Agreed next steps: send security docs, provision sandbox, run smoke test.

00:00 Sofia: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Sofia from Redwood — I'll run through a quick orientation and Ethan will jump into the demo and the retry lab.
00:12 Liam: Great, thanks. We only have about 45 minutes so high level first then deep dive.
00:20 Sofia: Super. Maya, Daniel, quick context — you mentioned chat-based summarization for patient notes and an internal triage assistant, can you confirm latency target and cost concerns?
00:38 Maya: Yeah, our target is sub-400ms p95 for short completions (one to two paragraphs) and then lower cost for bulk nightly batching jobs. We're also very strict on PHI handling and need to know retention and KMS stuff.
00:55 Sofia: Got it — we'll cover retention/KMS in the security slide and Ethan will show how hosted handles isolation and logs. Also we'll demo streaming, param tuning — temperature, top_p, max_tokens, and retry/backoff patterns.

01:05 Ethan: I'll share my screen, showing the Redwood Console sandbox with a hosted API key bound to a demo project. Note: this is a sandbox instance.
01:20 [screen share noise] 
01:28 Ethan: Starting with a simple chat prompt — system: "You are a medical summarizer. Summarize clinical note in 2-3 bullets." User payload is short. Now streaming is on, I set temperature 0.2 and max_tokens 180.
01:42 Maya: Quick Q — when you stream, do we get partial tokens as they generate? And do we need to handle replays if there's a mid-stream error?
01:52 Ethan: Yes, streaming yields deltas as pieces of text. On the client we surface a chunked stream. For mid-stream failures the recommended pattern is: 1) idempotency key per user request; 2) small client-side retry window with exponential backoff; 3) detect duplicate completions server-side using idempotency token. We'll show a code snippet for that.
02:15 Daniel: Are idempotency tokens required for every request? We have many concurrent short calls.
02:22 Ethan: Not required, but strongly recommended for critical flows. For best-effort UI flows you can skip, but for billing-sensitive or stateful ops you should include them. Also, if you rely on deterministic completions set temperature low and seed with structured prompts to reduce variance.

02:40 Ethan: Demo — toggling temperature to 0.9. Observe the streaming output becomes more exploratory, more filler and longer sentences; cost similar but more tokens sometimes. Lower temp 0.1 yields shorter, conservative outputs.
03:05 Maya: That matches our experiments. For nightly batch jobs we'd probably want temperature 0.0 and heavy batching to minimize token cost. Can Redwood help with batching suggestions?
03:17 Sofia: Yes, Redwood Optimize will recommend batching window sizes and quantization/mode for the model family based on your token distribution. In the console there's a suggestions card — we'll include a screenshot in the follow-up.

03:31 Ethan: Next — concurrency and timeouts. Hosted API has request timeout windows and recommended client timeouts. If you set a client timeout shorter than server SLO, you can get broken streams. For mobile clients we recommend progressive streaming + a short idempotency token so the server can finish even if the client disconnects.
03:55 Liam: What about retries? Do you recommend network-level retries on same idempotency key?
04:03 Ethan: Yes. Recommended pattern: exponential backoff with jitter, max 3 retries for transient 5xx errors, and immediate failover to a cheaper model variant for latency-sensitive paths. Redwood's smart routing can automatically fallback to a compatible model when the primary model is constrained.
04:20 Maya: Can you show an example of fallback?
04:25 Ethan: Sure — switching routing policy in the console from "latency-first" to "cost-aware fallback"; when primary model hits capacity we'll route to a slightly smaller quantized variant. Demo a synthetic load — you'll see console show a fallback event and the stream continues with the alternate model. Note: there can be slight distributional differences; Optimize will flag quality regressions if they exceed thresholds.

04:55 [15s silence while demo simulates load] 
05:10 Ethan: There — fallback triggered, stream continued. The text is a bit more concise; reason logged in the trace.
05:20 Maya: Nice. How do you surface those logs? We need audit trail for each token/request.
05:27 Ethan: Per-request tracing is available in Console logs— includes model id, variant, latency breakdown per stage (scheduling, token gen), and an optional redact/hyperlink to raw payload if you enable extended logging. For PHI-sensitive workloads you can keep only hashed traces and ship raw logs to your own S3 via the private deployment / log-forwarder.

05:50 Daniel: About retention — can we set zero retention for certain endpoints? We can't have any customer text persisted.
05:58 Sofia: Yes, hosted has a zero-retention option at the route level for enterprise customers with contractual SLAs. We'll attach the contract language and SOC2 controls. KMS integration: we support Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) and HSM-backed keys for Private and Dedicated customers; hosted supports cloud KMS options.
06:18 Liam: Good. Next — can you walk through the retry code pattern you recommended?
06:25 Ethan: Pulling up a snippet from the docs. Example pseudo-code: client sends POST with idempotency_key; on network timeout or HTTP 502/503/504 we do backoff (200ms -> 600ms -> 1800ms) with randomized jitter, and recheck request status endpoint if available. For streaming specifically, if you reconnect using the same idempotency key the server will either return cached completion or resume depending on prefix caching and model compatibility.
06:55 Maya: Prefix caching — is that per-account or global? How does it affect privacy?
07:02 Ethan: Prefix/KV cache is per-customer shard for hosted; it caches KV cache for recurring prompts to reduce token compute. It is encrypted at rest. For PHI you can opt out of caching per-route and also enable zero retention.
07:18 Maya: Okay. That's important.

07:25 Ethan: Now quick live failure modes lab — I'll simulate a transient 503 during streaming and show the client behavior.
07:32 [demo noise] 
07:37 Ethan: First run without idempotency key: the client loses stream and tries naive immediate retry — note you may get duplicate partial outputs and inconsistent state.
07:48 Daniel: Yeah that will break our UI.
07:50 Ethan: Second run with idempotency key and conservative backoff — server returns the same completion and we append only missing tokens; client de-dups partials. This improves user experience.
08:05 Maya: Any limits on length of idempotency keys or TTL?
08:10 Ethan: Key length limited to 128 chars; TTL configurable up to 72 hours for hosted. For long-running batch ops you can store results externally and use Redwood only for generation.

08:25 Ethan: Also show rate limiting and quotas — console exposes per-route token quotas and soft-limits. If you exceed quota we return 429s and a Retry-After header; retry policy should respect that header.
08:40 Liam: Do 429s count towards billing?
08:44 Sofia: No, 429s are not billable. We bill on accepted token generation. We'll send the billing FAQ as a follow-up.

08:52 Ethan: Quick note about model params — besides temperature and max_tokens, top_p, presence_penalty, frequency_penalty are available. There's also stop sequences and token_bias to bias particular tokens.
09:06 Maya: Token bias — can we nudge the model to avoid PHI or PII?
09:11 Ethan: You can set token_bias to heavily penalize tokens corresponding to names or SSN patterns, but that's heuristics not a replacement for classic PII redaction. For high assurance you should do post-processing filters and entity detection.

09:26 Ethan: Now the Console tour: route creation -> show fields for "streaming enabled", "idempotency enforcement", "retention policy", and drop-down for "fallback policy". I'll create a temporary route for "triage-summary" with retention zero and streaming on.
09:45 [typing sounds] 
09:52 Ethan: Route created. There's an SDK snippet ready to paste. I'll paste it in the chat.
09:58 [chat paste noise] 
10:05 Ethan: Code snippet for node (streaming):
     - create request with idempotency_key: uuidv4(), body: messages..., temperature: 0.2, max_tokens: 180, stream: true
     - handle 'delta' events and final 'done' event, handle network errors with backoff

10:30 Daniel: Would love a Python example for our backend.
10:33 Ethan: We'll attach both.

10:40 Maya: A few edge questions — does streaming incur more billing overhead vs non-streaming?
10:46 Sofia: No, billing is token-based at the same unit cost for tokens generated; streaming is just the transport. There can be slightly more egress (connection overhead) but token billing is primary.

10:58 Liam: On model variants — how big are the distributional differences when falling back? Are there tools to detect regressions?
11:06 Ethan: Optimize hooks run evals on your prompt sets. You can register a golden prompt set and Redwood will run regressions when fallbacks happen or when you roll model versions. If regression threshold exceeds X% we'll alert and you can auto-fallback to previous variant.
11:20 Maya: Sounds good. For our nightly jobs we want deterministic outputs, so we'll pin model version and use quantized variant.
11:27 Ethan: Right — pin versions on the route level so rollouts don't surprise batch jobs.

11:34 Sofia: Final recap and next steps — Ethan will provision sandbox, Sofia will email security docs and pricing, Maya will provide payload stats. We'll schedule a 30-minute follow-up after the smoke test. Anything else?
11:52 Liam: One last thing: does Redwood support SSO for consoles?
11:58 Sofia: Yes, SAML/SSO + RBAC for Console and API keys can be scoped by route. We'll paste SSO setup guide.
12:10 Maya: Thanks — this was helpful.
12:14 Sofia: Great, thanks everyone. We'll follow up by Friday.
